name: Fatima Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting this in. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the month. I'm farm manager for a small family company that farms about 900 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, spread over four farms. In spring it's spraying and fertiliser, in August it's harvest, sixteen-hour days, and in winter it's machinery repairs and planning. Today I was in the workshop fixing a sprayer boom, then on the phone to the grain merchant about prices.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Harvest, even though it nearly kills me. Watching the combine fill a trailer at sunset, knowing the year's work is in. And I like the numbers side, weirdly. Working out whether to sell now or store and wait is like a game where the stakes are real.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay doesn't match the job. I manage three full-timers and two seasonal drivers, and I'm on less than the grain merchant's junior trader. My partner Ravi drives a grain lorry, so our money goes up and down with the same harvest. We've usually got under a month's bills saved. One bad year and we feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to check a spray label or write up a report for the company directors. It's a tool, like the GPS on the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes almost nothing. What decides my year is the weather, the grain price and the cost of fertiliser. A better search engine won't make it rain in May.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as usual. Keep using the AI tool for paperwork when it's quicker, maybe use it to compare grain price reports. Ask the directors for a rise at the annual review in October, with the yields to back it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is basically today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You compared AI to the tractor GPS. When did you start using GPS?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was 22, on my first job. The old manager didn't trust it and drove by eye. Within a season everyone on that farm used it because it saved fuel and overlaps. That's how I take up most things: once it's shown it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI tool ever get things wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It once told me a spray was approved for oilseed rape when it wasn't. I checked the label like you always should. So I use it to save time, not to make decisions.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy, a tool like the GPS on the tractor. I use one now and then to check spray labels and write reports for the directors.
S0.think: It changes almost nothing for me. My year is decided by the weather, grain prices and fertiliser costs, and a better search engine won't make it rain in May.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for paperwork when it's quicker and to compare grain price reports. Asks the directors for a rise at the October review, backed by yield figures.
S0.feel: Calm; this is essentially life as it is now.
S0.quote: A better search engine won't make it rain in May.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is practical, numerate and unexcited, with a clear rule: adopt once something has proved itself, check its work, keep the decisions. The wrong spray answer gave her a healthy distrust. Her money worries are tied to harvest because her partner hauls grain too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is manageable if companies keep training people. I might say something at the farmers' discussion group about apprentices. Not online, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it might even help me a bit. The agronomist, the crop adviser we pay, might use AI to cover more farms, which could cut our fees. But fewer beginners hired means fewer tractor drivers coming through, and finding harvest drivers is already a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try any AI crop planning tool once a couple of neighbours had used it for a season. I'd push the company to take on one apprentice driver, maybe split the cost with the farm next door. And I'd start booking harvest drivers in January instead of June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy about finding people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time you couldn't find a harvest driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago, a driver dropped out the week before harvest. I drove the grain trailer myself for eighteen days and managed the whole farm from the cab on my phone. We got it all in, but I lost about four kilos, and Ravi said I looked like a ghost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a slower world change how you see your own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In ten years, I'd want to be running something bigger, or maybe renting my own land. Slow change gives me time to plan that. I'd rather the world moved at my speed than me at its.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is manageable if companies keep training people. I'd raise apprentices at the farmers' discussion group rather than online.
S1.think: It might help me a bit if the crop adviser uses AI to cover more farms and charges less. But fewer beginners means fewer tractor drivers, and harvest drivers are already hard to find.
S1.do: Tries an AI crop planning tool after neighbours have used it for a season. Pushes for an apprentice driver, possibly shared with the next farm, and starts booking harvest drivers in January.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little uneasy about finding staff.
S1.quote: I'd rather the world moved at my speed than me at its.
S1.fieldNote: She sees small gains and small risks, and weighs them evenly. The harvest story shows how much depends on her personally. Slow change suits her ambition of one day farming her own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. Office workers need help, but you can't ban the technology either. I'd say we should help people move into work that's short of hands, like farming, and pay for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it might help me find staff. A laid-off office worker who wants to be outside could make a good tractor driver with a season's training. But it also means the grain merchant and the company's accounts office get leaner, and some of that work lands on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd advertise for harvest drivers in places where office people look for work, and offer a two-week course in spring. I'd let the AI assistant do more of the company reports. And I'd ask Ravi's haulage firm if they're hiring more, since everyone still needs grain moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not worried for myself. More curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to make the rules in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd trust whoever shows the numbers. If someone says 'this will cost this and help this many people', I'll listen. Anyone who just shouts, I tune out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture a laid-off accountant turning up for your tractor course. What happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First day, he'd be nervous about the size of the thing. By day four, he'd be better at the record-keeping than any of my lads. I'd want him for the grain store, actually. Funny how it'd work out.

S2.say: I'd say both sides have a point: office workers need help, but you can't ban the technology. We should help people move into work that's short of hands, like farming, and pay for the training.
S2.think: It might help me find staff, since some laid-off office workers would want outdoor work. But leaner offices at the merchant and the company mean more admin lands on me.
S2.do: Advertises harvest driving where office workers look for jobs and offers a two-week spring course. Gives the AI assistant more of the reports and asks her partner's haulage firm about hiring.
S2.feel: Uneasy but more curious than scared.
S2.quote: By day four, he'd be better at the record-keeping than any of my lads. I'd want him for the grain store, actually.
S2.fieldNote: She is the first farmer I've heard see an office downturn partly as a hiring chance. Her middle-ground view rests on evidence and costs rather than loyalty to a side. She thinks like a manager here, more than a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible deal: some tax on the winners, but not so much that nobody builds anything. I'd say that to anyone who asked, and plenty of people at the discussion group would disagree with me from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is probably safe, but my plans aren't. I wanted to rent land of my own in a few years. If land prices boom with everything else, that's gone. The new money buys farms as investments, and someone like me with under a month saved can't compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the directors and ask about a share arrangement, where I farm a block of land as a partner instead of renting it outright. I'd spend the winter learning the AI tools for farm budgets properly, so I can prove I'm worth it. And I'd keep ten percent of every pay cheque aside, however tight it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared of losing my job, scared of being stuck in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten percent of every pay cheque, on your wage. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. We'd give up the holiday we've planned for two years, a week by the sea in September after harvest. Ravi would be gutted. But that's what ten percent costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the ladder were pulled up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one person. The system rewards people who already own things. That's not a conspiracy, it's just how it works when prices boom. I'd want the rules to give people like me a step up, not a handout.

S3.say: I'd say we need a sensible deal: some tax on the winners, but not so much that nobody builds anything. People on both sides at the discussion group would disagree with me.
S3.think: My job is probably safe but my plans aren't. If land prices boom, new money buys farms as investments, and with under a month saved I can't compete to rent my own.
S3.do: Asks the directors about a share farming deal for a block of land. Learns AI farm budgeting tools over the winter, and saves ten percent of every pay cheque by giving up a planned holiday.
S3.feel: Anxious, less about losing the job than about being stuck in it.
S3.quote: Not scared of losing my job, scared of being stuck in it.
S3.fieldNote: Her worry is ambition blocked rather than income lost, which is new among these interviews. She explains the boom as a system effect, not a villain. Giving up the September holiday makes the cost real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robot tractors aren't science fiction, they're already being tested. I'd say farms need a plan for the people, not just the machines. I'd say it at the discussion group, and probably to the directors in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job changes more than it disappears. A self-driving tractor still needs someone deciding what it does and fixing it when it gets stuck in a wet corner. But my three full-timers? Two of them, maybe all three, would go. And Ravi's lorry could drive itself too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see the robots working on a big estate first, probably next county. Then I'd propose to the directors that we bring them in slowly, one machine at a time, and that I train the full-timers to supervise them. And Ravi and I would cut back hard, because if his job goes we're on one income with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. For me, uneasy. For Ravi and the lads, alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the full-timers would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Geoff. He's 58, a brilliant driver, and he hates his phone. I don't think he'd learn to supervise a robot, and I don't think anyone would hire him at 58. I'd fight to keep him on for the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job changes more than it disappears. What if the directors decide they don't need a manager either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be looking for a manager's job on a bigger farm. There'd be fewer of those too. I'd try not to think about that one too much, honestly.

S4.say: I'd say robot tractors aren't science fiction and are already being tested. Farms need a plan for the people, not just the machines, and I'd put that to the directors in writing.
S4.think: My job changes more than it disappears, because self-driving tractors still need someone to decide and fix things. But two or three of my full-timers would go, and Ravi's lorry could drive itself too.
S4.do: Visits an estate already using robots, then proposes bringing them in one machine at a time with the full-timers trained to supervise. Cuts household spending hard in case her partner's driving job goes.
S4.feel: Uneasy for herself but alarmed for her partner and her team.
S4.quote: Geoff. He's 58, a brilliant driver, and he hates his phone.
S4.fieldNote: She is the manager who might survive while her team doesn't, and she knows it. The household risk is doubled because her partner drives a lorry. She briefly admits she avoids thinking about the worst case for herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because of Ravi and the lads. What would help is training paid partly by the machinery companies and partly by government, so people like Geoff can stay on in some role. And some way for young farmers to get land, like share farming deals that are easier to set up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about land. Everyone asks about jobs, but in farming, whoever owns the land decides everything. If you want to know who wins, ask who owns the fields.

headlineQuote: If you want to know who wins, ask who owns the fields.
portrait: Fatima Nakamura is 27 and manages 900 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape for a family farming company, living with her partner Ravi, a grain lorry driver. She's calm, numerate and even-handed, adopting tools like GPS and AI once they've proved themselves and always checking their work. In the middle scenarios she even sees a chance to hire laid-off office workers, but in the fast scenario her real fear is being stuck, priced out of ever farming her own land. Robots threaten her team and her partner more than herself, and she'd fight to keep her oldest driver, Geoff. She keeps coming back to land ownership as the thing that decides who wins.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because her partner's driving job and her team's jobs would be at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid partly by machinery companies and partly by government so older workers can stay on, and easier share farming deals so young farmers can get land.
